fields.v: Weinberger, S., Hozez, A. (2026). Prompt-Induced Waste in Coding Agents: Reasoning, Effort, Harness Design, and End-to-End Cost. A Preregistered Benchmark with Harness Extensions. arXiv:2608.01347v6 [cs.CL], 10 Sep 2026
Preprint — arXiv:2608.01347v6 [cs.CL]; no venue stated
Industry: PointFive (both authors)

Compares; secondary: Proposes an approach — preregistered paired experiments comparing prompt-wording variants, inference-effort levels and agent harnesses (PI.DEV, Claude Code, DeepSeek Harness) on cost and success; proposes a trajectory cost model with cost per successful task as terminal metric, benchmark reporting requirements, and the training problem for an adaptive efficiency controller (design only, not evaluated)
fields.why: Main nature 'Compares' is clear. Two candidates for the secondary nature: the trained adaptive controller of Section 8 is design only ('not evaluated', pp. 8, 11), but the rule-based controller arms (policy, rewrite, effort, full) inherited from the authors' 'frozen activation benchmark' are evaluated in Sec. 6.1 and App. O; alternatively the cost model (Sec. 7) and reporting requirements (Sec. 9) support 'Proposes an evaluation method'. The choice decides Q13
fields.doubt: Há um controlador avaliado (braços policy/rewrite/effort, secção 6.1 e apêndice O) e outro só desenhado (secção 8). Decide se a natureza secundária é 'Proposes an approach' ou 'Proposes an evaluation method'; isso decide Q13.

fields.v: No SDD approach. Factors compared: (a) 18 frozen prompt variants (9 primary semantically controlled, e.g. precise baseline, multiple approaches, deep thinking, max certainty, bounded efficiency; 7 stress variants; 2 harness-axis); (b) explicit effort levels (low/high/xhigh/max); (c) harnesses: PI.DEV 0.82.1, Claude Code 2.1.220 (via LiteLLM 1.93.0 gateway, and native), DeepSeek Harness (dsh) 0.1.0rc7. Efficiency controller arms in the dsh extension: policy (efficiency policy appended to system persona), rewrite (wrapper prompt correction), effort (adaptive reasoningEffort override), full (all three); no version

N/A (no specification artefacts). Each task prompt states one objective, explicit acceptance criteria and the test command; the bounded-efficiency template adds scope, a smallest-sufficient-change criterion and a stopping rule
N/A (no development flow prescribed; the paper models the agent trajectory: model requests, reasoning, tool actions, edits, retries, stopping)
None (automated runs; humans only for blind validation of trace labels)
N/A (prompt wording, effort setting and harness varied; no approach exercised)
Not classifiable (no specification approach); authors do not use SDD terms

Existing code: small deterministic coding tasks on frozen fixtures that fail visible tests before the fix (bugs/features, <= 4 files); repository-scale issue resolution on a hard SWE-bench Verified slice

Core benchmark: 24 tasks (8 low/8 medium/8 high; 9 Python, 9 JavaScript, 6 Go; 16 development + 8 holdout), 4,644 valid runs, 2,801 annotated traces. Extensions: Kimi-K3 96 runs; Sonnet 5 cross-provider 162 runs; robustness 2,105 runs; adaptive-compute 320 runs on 8 tasks; SWE-effort 25 instances (2-21 files, >= 40 lines, 8 repositories), 150 cells; dsh 75 runs on 5 tasks
General small coding tasks and open-source repositories (SWE-bench Verified); not domain-specific
N/A (no human participants)

Reasoning tokens, visible output tokens, uncached and cached input, cache reads/writes, actual billed cost at pinned catalog prices, estimated no-cache cost, cost per successful task (CPS), cost per resolved task; wall time; turns; tool calls; tool-induced model cost (bounded 4-12%); fixed prefix size
Task success on visible plus hidden deterministic tests; SWE-bench resolved rate with the official Docker evaluator; hidden-test-only failures
Out-of-scope changes (git diff vs allowed paths); diff width; scope compliance
None

Primary outcome: paired reasoning ratio vs same-block baseline median; trace mechanisms (discarded branches, redundant re-verification, unsupported assumptions, functional units) from a condition-blind judge; tool calls by type, duplicate reads, repeated searches, repeated green test runs, time to first edit; within-cell cost coefficient of variation and success unanimity across repetitions

Automatic: provider-side usage objects captured by two logging reverse proxies around the gateway (gateway drops reasoning detail; Claude Code's own cost report measured at 3.5x true cost, so not used); deterministic tool taxonomy extractor (unit-tested, validated on blind hand labels); hidden deterministic evaluators; SWE-bench Docker evaluator. LLM judge (condition-blind, evidence quotes) for trace annotation, validated against researcher-blind labels (84.9% within +-1; kappa 0.28-0.68)

Success criterion stated by the authors: per-task success on visible + hidden deterministic tests (official SWE-bench Docker evaluator for the hard slice); no success-rate threshold for a configuration. Cost criterion stated by the authors for prompt variants: 'wasteful' when median reasoning ratio > 1.5 with CI lower bound > 1.1, no material success gain, on multiple tasks (p. 13). (1) PI.DEV 0.82.1 + six Together-served open models (DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi-K2.6, Kimi-K2.7-Code, Nemotron-3-Ultra, Inkling, GLM-5.2), holdout: multiple approaches 2.4-7.4x reasoning, confirmed wasteful on 6/6 (aggregate success 95.2% vs 96.5% baseline over 225 paired blocks); deep thinking 1.6-2.2x wasteful where selected; bounded efficiency neutral on 6/6 (GLM-5.2 0.48x). Quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors; cost does not work for branching/deep-thinking/certainty variants (wasteful by the authors' rule), works for bounded efficiency (confirmed neutral). (2) Claude Code 2.1.220 via LiteLLM gateway + the same open models: ~100% pilot success, 5-30x cost per success vs PI.DEV, 10-41 turns vs 5-7. Verdicts: no criterion stated by the authors. (3) PI.DEV + Kimi-K3: 72/72 success; multiple approaches 16.6x, deep thinking 14.8x vs own (low) baseline; bounded efficiency 0.89x. Quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors; cost as in (1). (4) PI.DEV + claude-sonnet-5 and native Claude Code + claude-sonnet-5 (162 runs, all valid): multiple approaches 2.70x / 2.52x output tokens; max certainty 4.13x output and 2.7x no-cache CPS under native Claude Code; native Claude Code baseline CPS ~15x PI.DEV. Quality verdict: no criterion stated by the authors; cost does not work for these variants. (5) Adaptive-compute campaign, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5, 8 tasks: all solved at low effort; static max effort 1.5-2.8x CPS with no success gain; bounded efficiency caused 3/5 hidden-test failures on the ambiguous task. Verdicts: no criterion stated by the authors. (6) Claude Code 2.1.220 + Claude Opus 5, SWE hard slice: resolved 17/18/16 of 25 at low/high/xhigh, CPS $0.75/$1.89/$3.62. (7) Claude Code 2.1.220 + Claude Sonnet 5: 12/19/17 of 25, CPS $1.76/$2.32/$3.00 (high vs low p=0.016; xhigh vs low n.s. after Holm). Verdicts (6)-(7): no criterion stated by the authors. (8) DeepSeek Harness 0.1.0rc7 + Sonnet 5, 5 tasks x 3 reps: baseline $0.2753/run, policy -23.2%, rewrite -23.4%, effort -74.7%, full -82.2%, all 15/15 success (Claude Code activation benchmark: effort -19%, full -27%). Verdicts: no criterion stated by the authors
fields.why: Values match Table 3, Table 5 and Appendices J, K, M, N, O. Quality is left 'no criterion stated' because the authors give per-task hidden tests but no success-rate threshold per configuration; cost verdicts use the authors' preregistered 'wasteful' rule (ratio > 1.5, CI lower bound > 1.1, no success gain; A.5), but mapping 'neutral' to 'works' and applying the rule to output-token ratios for Sonnet 5 are extractor judgements
fields.doubt: Os autores só dão sucesso por tarefa (testes ocultos), sem limiar por configuração; o custo usa a regra 'wasteful' (A.5). Decide se 'neutral' equivale a 'works' e se a qualidade fica 'no criterion stated'.

fields.v: Paired within task-model-harness blocks; prompt variants alter only the user instruction (objective, acceptance criteria and test command verbatim, validated automatically); frozen fixtures with hidden tests absent from the workspace; per-model top variants selected on development data and re-run on an 8-task frozen holdout (5 reps, n=40 per cell). Baseline: precise baseline prompt; own-harness baseline for controller arms; low effort for effort campaigns. Held constant: task, model, harness, nominal effort within a block; for dsh, model, tasks, prompts, evaluators and controller logic fixed while only the harness changes. Repetitions: up to 5 per cell; second repetitions on SWE discordant pairs. Statistics: task-clustered bootstrap CIs, sign-flip permutation, McNemar, Holm. Preregistered hypotheses H1-H8, H12-H17 frozen in the repository; extensions frozen before results. Human intervention: none

Prompt content, not length, drives work: multiple approaches 2.4-7.4x reasoning (holdout-confirmed, no success benefit: 96.5% vs 95.2%, discordant 26:13 favouring baseline; easy cells 98.8% -> 96.4%, p~.003); deep thinking 1.6-2.2x; certainty 1.3-1.9x with redundant re-verification; verbatim repetition ~1x; bounded efficiency neutral-or-better. Redundant verification level 3+ costs 18x clean-run median. Harness gap larger: Claude Code 12-15x larger prefix, 2-7x more turns, 5-30x cost per success vs PI.DEV at comparable success; prompt effects do not transfer across harnesses. Effort: on hard SWE tasks Sonnet 5 benefits from high effort (7 rescues, 0 regressions), Opus 5 does not (low on the frontier); xhigh dominated. Harness x effort interaction: effort control saves ~75% under dsh vs ~19% under Claude Code. Caching cuts ~61% of the bill without changing behaviour

Distinguished prompt variants, harnesses and effort levels on cost at high success; holdout and paraphrase/repetition analyses confirmed direction stability (one feature failed holdout; hard-cell branching signal failed cross-fitting). Limitations stated: high success ceilings limit detectable success effects to >= ~2.8 pp; adaptive-compute tasks produced no baseline failures; effort control did not reliably modulate computation on the Together-served open models; gateway can silently drop tool schemas or reasoning items; trace claims rely on visible reasoning and an imperfect judge; Claude Code arms smaller by design

Visible reasoning not faithful to latent computation; Sonnet 5 traces unrecoverable; per-turn cost attribution unavailable (tool-induced cost bounded 4-12%); no local resource telemetry; post-success based on visible-test proxy; tool counts zero-inflated, some effects only directional; tasks small (<= 4 files) with high ceilings, may not transfer to long-horizon production agents; catalog prices at collection time; branching on architecture-dependent tasks untested; dsh extension one model, five ceiling tasks, no DeepSeek models, no hook arm, dsh capabilities not varied. Future work: hard SWE-bench slice under dsh with Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 crossing harness and effort; ablations of context-crossing and orchestration; train and evaluate the adaptive controller with non-inferiority checks

Replication package: https://github.com/PointFiveLabs/prompt-efficiency-benchmark (fixtures, hidden evaluators, prompts, runners, telemetry, analysis code). Pre-registration claimed: hypotheses, metrics and thresholds frozen in the repository before results (repository commits, not an independent registry); some extensions are post-registration; SWE-effort budget cap amended from $250 to $300 before outcomes were evaluated. Programming languages: Python, JavaScript, Go (core tasks); SWE-bench Verified (Python). Same authors as 'Token Reduction Is Not Cost Reduction'. Text says 'six open-weight models' in the core design but 'seven models with provider-exposed reasoning text' / 'all seven open-weight models' (Kimi-K3 added post-registration). Claude Code test-call share given as 'approximately half' (Sec. 6), 53-56% (Fig. 2) and ~52% (App. D). The Claude Code activation benchmark with the same controller (effort -19%, full -27%) is cited but its design is not reported in this paper. Absolute per-run costs small; multiplicative effects not extrapolated

Partly (0.5): authors (PointFive) independent of the harness and model vendors, but the efficiency controller arms (policy, rewrite, effort) appear to be the authors' own (not attributed to a third party)
fields.why: The controller arms (policy, rewrite, effort, full) come from the authors' 'frozen activation benchmark' (Sec. 6.1, App. O) and are compared with each harness baseline, but the paper never states explicitly who built them; if they are the authors' own, Partly (rule of 2026-11-23), otherwise Yes
fields.doubt: O artigo não diz explicitamente quem criou os braços do controlador (policy, rewrite, effort). Se forem dos autores, Q12 é Partly; se não, Yes. Confirma no apêndice O e na secção 6.1.

fields.v: Partly (0.5): proposed adaptive controller stated to need only logged telemetry and a small tabular/gradient-boosted model, no extra LLM; but it is not built, and data, compute and cost requirements are not quantified
fields.why: Applies only if 'Proposes an approach' is kept. Section 8 states the trained controller needs only logged telemetry and a small tabular or gradient-boosted model, no extra LLM, but it is not built or quantified; the evaluated rule-based arms (efficiency policy text, prompt rewrite, effort override) need no extra infrastructure, which would argue for a higher score if they count as the approach
fields.doubt: Só se aplica com 'Proposes an approach'. O controlador da secção 8 não foi construído; os braços avaliados (policy, rewrite, effort) quase não exigem infraestrutura. Decide qual conta e escolhe Partly, Yes ou N/A.
